title: Algorithmic Complexity
learning_outcomes: Explain the central rule or purpose of algorithmic complexity using at least one correct term from the lesson.
Interpret or adapt a small Kotlin example that demonstrates algorithmic complexity.
Identify one relevant edge case, debugging step, or version/platform constraint.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will learn **Algorithmic Complexity** as part of **Software Engineering, Security, and Performance**. Choose an algorithm by correctness and input constraints, then reason about time and space complexity before attempting optimization. Use the subtopics—Big-O Notation, Time and Space Complexity, Analyzing Collection Operations—as a checklist: predict what the example will do, then verify it in a project configured for the target platform.
content.why_it_matters: Professional applications need repeatable tests, clear APIs, dependable dependencies, security checks, and observable failures. Apply this concept in small steps before integrating it into a larger project.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Choose an algorithm by correctness and input constraints, then reason about time and space complexity before attempting optimization.

content_blocks.title: How to reason about it
content_blocks.text: Start with big-o notation. Then compare it with time and space complexity. Identify the input, state, dependency, or branch that determines the result. The snippet is a static reference for CodeLeaf and is not executed in the lesson page.

items.title: Big-O Notation
items.text: Big-O Notation is one part of algorithmic complexity. Connect its definition to the example, identify the input/state it changes, and verify the expected behavior with a small test case.

items.title: Time and Space Complexity
items.text: Time and Space Complexity should be evaluated against input size, allocation behavior, and workload. Start with a correctness test and reproducible measurement; choose the simplest implementation that meets the requirement.

items.title: Analyzing Collection Operations
items.text: Analyzing Collection Operations is best learned by tracing a small collection before and after the operation. Check ordering, duplicate handling, empty inputs, and whether the API returns a new value or mutates a mutable receiver.

content_blocks.code:
fun linearSearch(values: List<Int>, target: Int): Int = values.indexOf(target)

fun main() = println(linearSearch(listOf(4, 7, 9), 7))
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run in the project that declares the necessary JVM, coroutine, networking, database, or serialization dependencies. Never commit real secrets.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the documented starting values, rerun the smallest test, and compare the result with the expected output. If behavior differs, check the compiler/plugin/runtime versions and the active target before changing more than one thing.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake to avoid
content_blocks.text: Algorithmic Complexity removes the need to test boundary conditions or verify the chosen runtime/library version.

content_blocks.title: Troubleshooting and reset
content_blocks.text: If the example fails, first confirm which runtime/project type the snippet requires. Read the first useful compiler or runtime message, check imports and declared dependencies, reduce the example to a minimal case, and rerun. For target-specific code, use the target toolchain rather than assuming a console or browser runner can execute it.

items.title: Explain
items.text: Describe the main rule of algorithmic complexity in your own words.

items.title: Apply
items.text: Change one input or condition and predict the result before running it.

items.title: Verify
items.text: Check one edge case and the official reference for the selected Kotlin/runtime version.

content.task: Try it yourself: create a small variation that demonstrates algorithmic complexity. Write down your predicted result first, run it in the correct local project, then explain one boundary case involving big-o notation.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain algorithmic complexity without copying the lesson wording.
